So this is a refresh from curfew 150.
 If you don't know these words, it's okay, but it would be good to be familiar with them
 in the weeks forward, just because it makes reading anything to do with the criminal law
 a lot more simple, because if you get some of these words wrong, particularly like prosecution
 and defendants, it means you'll read the entire case wrong and you just waste it a bit of time.
 So things such as charge, you know, so that's a formal declaration of someone being charged
 of an offence or being recognized as potentially having done that offence.
 Someone has made a complaint and there's a sufficient enough amount of evidence to engage
 in an investigation or a trial against them.
 So offence is basically just like a category, like what crime you're committed with or what
 crime you're charged with.
 That one's fairly straightforward.
 Prosecution, you remember, in a first instance trial, that is the, in criminal law most commonly
 the state, that is the party that is giving evidence in order to see that person being
 committed of the offence or giving evidence in order to prosecute them.
 And then there's conviction, which is after your trial, if you're found guilty, you're
 convicted of the offence.
 I think the main, like, the best one to know is when someone's charged with an offence
 versus when someone is convicted with an offence.
 If they're charged with the offence, they actually haven't been found to commit it,
 to have committed it, sorry, and they're still technically presumed innocent.
 Then a trial will happen, if they're found guilty, then they're convicted, then they'll
 go to prison or what have you.
